newsitem.title: USA: Dollar hit by slide in U.S. stocks, strong data in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Dollar hit by slide in U.S. stocks, strong data in Europe.

text.p: The dollar fell broadly on Thursday, dragged lower by a slide in Wall Street stocks, signs of economic strength in Europe and more verbal attempts by German central bank officials to tame the dollar's recent strength.

"The dollar's drop is a combination of profit-taking along with uncertainty about the future," said Hans Boman, chief spot dealer at Swedbank in New York, pointing to a fall of over 110 points in the Dow Jones industrial average.
The blue-chip index ended 92.75 lower at 6,927.38.
"It's difficult to tell what is going to happen from here and the dollar's flying up and down," he added.
Robust results from an index which tracks West German business activity and solid German money supply growth in January bolstered the mark at the dollar's expense.
The Ifo index rose to 93.3 in January from December's 90.0 while Germany's M3 money supply grew an annualized 11.7 percent in January since the fourth quarter of 1996.

"The German M3 money supply and Ifo survey were stronger than expected and that has diminished any real potential for an imminent rate cut in Germany," said Mike Malpede, senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group Ltd. in Chicago.
The dollar fell to its lowest level since Feb. 10 against the yen, closing at 122.45 yen, more than two yen below 124.55 late Wednesday. Against the mark, the dollar fell to 1.6835 from 1.6980.

The dollar was also hit by another call from Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer for an end to the dollar's rise against the mark. Tietmeyer voiced similar cries a number of times earlier this week, dealers said.

Tietmeyer said, in a taped interview for Hungarian radio, that the dollar's recent gains were a correction, "but we are not interested in a correction process that would go beyond tolerable limits". Tietmeyer added that a German interest rate cut was not likely in the short run.

The dollar also fell victim to a surge in the mark against the Norwegian crown after Norway's central bank surprised the markets by announcing it would resume foreign currency purchases. On Jan. 10, the bank had said it would curb intervention in the currency market.

Norway's central bank stressed it will resume foreign currency purchases, but not "as exchange market interventions," a subtle distinction which led to market confusion immediately following the announcement.
The mark also benefitted from a sharp drop in the British pound following news the Confederation of British Industry had cut its economic growth forecast, citing the pound's strength.
The CBI cut its 1997 Gross Domestic Production forecast to 2.8 percent from 3.1 percent and its inflation forecast to 2.2 percent from 2.5 percent.
"The mark's gains against sterling have undermined the dollar against the mark," Malpede said.

Meanwhile, the Japanese yen strengthened on speculation, later denied by a Ministry of Finance official, that the Japanese government was considering allocating new public funds to buy collateralized land formerly owned by troubled financial firms. The prospect of future monetary aid to Japan's troubled banking sector helped the yen, dealers said.

Also hurting the dollar against the yen was the movement of key short-term interest rates in Japan. The Japanese call rate rose above the nation's discount rate, an unusual relationship which suggests there is some room for the dollar to fall against the yen, analysts said.

The dollar received a brief lift after a strong report concerning U.S. business conditions from the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia. The Philadelphia index climbed to 17.4 in February, beating expectations for a 10.0 reading and January's 11.3 showing.
In other trading, the dollar fell to 1.4767 Swiss francs from 1.4857, but rose to Canadian $1.3615 from $1.3600. Sterling fell to $1.6114 from $1.6163.
